## The problem

All my career I've had a club theme or university colours to base my visuals and decks on. When I decided to build a portfolio, I was a bit flummoxed. This work needed to look distinct to me, and there was nothing to borrow.

A consistent theme matters a lot when delivering insight, because charts made in different tools drift apart. A ggplot in a report, a Shiny app and a slide deck each end up with their own colours and fonts, and colour starts to mean nothing in particular. The reader has to work out what to look at every time.

I wanted one set of rules that every output inherits automatically, so the design decisions are made once and the reader's attention goes straight to the point.

## The approach

Having been through [Andy Kirk's data visualisation training](https://visualisingdata.com/), I care as much about every chart telling a story as about charts looking consistent. Slate and Signal is built on that. The design decisions are made once, and each one exists to point the reader at what matters.

- **One accent, everything else grey.** The eye picks out whatever is different before the reader has consciously started looking. So signal teal (#009999) is kept for the one point of the chart, and everything that supports it sits in context grey (#B8C0C9).
- **Titles state the takeaway.** "High-speed running by player" names the topic. "Player 3 is back above their normal range" tells you what to think, and the chart then backs it up.
- **Defined once, used everywhere.** Every colour, font and size lives in a single tokens file. That one file generates the R theme, the Quarto styles, the Python helpers and the Streamlit configuration, so a report, an app and a deck can't drift apart.
- **Colours keep their meaning.** Categorical colours follow a fixed order, so the same series is the same colour in every chart. Status colours are only ever used for status.
- **Readable by everyone.** The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) set a minimum contrast between text and its background so people with low vision can still read it. Level AA, the standard most organisations work to, asks for a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text. Every text colour here meets it, which is why links use a darker teal (#007A7A) than the chart accent.
- **Safe for colour blindness.** Around [1 in 12 men](https://www.colourblindawareness.org/colour-blindness/) has some form of colour vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green. In a coaching staff, that's likely to be someone in the room. Every categorical colour was checked under simulations of the three main types (deutan, protan and tritan) so no two series look the same. Status colours never rely on colour alone either: in range, monitor and out of range always come with an icon and a word.

Inter carries the text and JetBrains Mono the code. Every rule has a light and a dark version, so the system holds in either theme.

## The palette


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/palette-1.svg){fig-alt='The Slate and Signal palette: brand colours, six categorical colours, a sequential teal scale and three status colours.'}
:::
:::


Slate gives structure, **signal teal** is the single accent, and a cool grey called **context** is used for everything that supports the message rather than being the message. Status colours are reserved for state (in range, monitor, out of range) and always appear with an icon or a word, never colour alone.

## Built to be readable by everyone

Every text colour was checked against both background colours using the WCAG contrast formula, and the categorical colours were checked under simulated colour-vision deficiency so no two series collapse into the same colour. ## The core rule: grey for context, signal for the point

The same data, drawn with default settings and then with the system. The default gives every player a different colour, so nothing stands out. With the system, the one player the chart is about is the only thing in colour, and the title says what the reader should take away.

## Style as code

The rules live in one tokens file and are packaged for each tool I use, so a chart picks up the system with a line or two:

```r
source("R/theme_md.R")

ggplot(df, aes(session, hsr, colour = player)) +
  geom_line() +
  md_highlight("Player 3") +   # grey for everyone except the focus
  theme_md()                   # type, gridlines, titles and captions
```

The same values drive a matplotlib and Plotly theme for Python, a Streamlit configuration, a Quarto slide theme, a PowerPoint template and this website.

## What I'd do next

Package the R theme as a small installable package with its own tests, so colleagues could adopt it with `library(mdtheme)` and get updates automatically.
